newsitem.title: USA: Crop prices tumble after bearish government data.
newsitem.headline: Crop prices tumble after bearish government data.

text.p: Surprising increases in U.S. government crop estimates launched a wave of selling in commodity markets Friday, forcing prices sharply lower for cotton, corn, orange juice and soybeans.

The declines were reflected in the Commodity Research Bureau's index, which fell 1.81 points Friday to 245.57. The index averages prices for 17 commodities and is often used as an indicator of inflationary trends.

Cotton futures at the New York Cotton Exchange fell 2.50 cents per pound early Friday, erasing gains from a month-long rally. Traders were shocked when the government raised its crop estimate and slashed usage.
"This report is not neutral but decisively bearish," said Sharon Johnson, an analyst with Frank Schneider and Co. Inc.

The Agriculture Department estimated the U.S. cotton crop at 18.189 million 480-pound bales, vs. its September estimate of 17.90 million. Ending stocks, the remaining supply after mill and export needs are met, were increased to 4.5 million bales from 3.6 million in September.
In early afternoon, NYCE cotton for December delivery was down 2.10 cents at 73.30 cents per pound after earlier falling as low as 72.90 cents. The daily limit is 3 cents.

Corn and soybean futures sped lower at the Chicago Board of Trade after the Agriculture Department increased U.S. crop estimates to 9.012 billion bushels of corn and 2.346 billion of soybeans, up from 8.803 billion and 2.27 billion, respectively.
The corn estimate would be the third largest U.S crop in history and the soybean estimate would be the second largest.
"There's nothing friendly about the corn or bean numbers," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities.
Roose noted that the corn and soybean harvests are under way in the Midwest, which seasonally force prices lower.
Corn for December delivery fell 6 cents Friday afternoon to $2.84 per bushel. Soybeans for November delivery fell the daily 30 cent limit to $7.00-1/4 per bushel.
The selling spilled into Canada, where prices for canola, an oilseed that competes with soybeans, fell the maximum $10 per metric ton limit at the Winnipeg Commodity Exchange.

In its first crop estimate of the year, the Agriculture Department estimated the U.S. orange crop at 220 million 20-pound boxes, which exceeded many trade estimates and exceeds last year's crop of 203.2 million.

That news, coupled with reports of slowing demand, fuelled selling of frozen concentrated orange juice futures at the New York Cotton Exchange. The November contract was down 2.60 cents at 109.60 cents a pound. The daily limit is 10 cents for November, and 5 cents for other contracts.
